title: Paul's list (2 Corinthians 11:24–28)
hookLine: beaten, shipwrecked, hungry, cold, and still going

lines: A RÉSUMÉ IS A LIST OF WINS.
cards: A résumé is a list of wins. Degrees, titles, the big project you led. Nobody puts was fired twice at the top.

In his second letter to the church in Corinth, Paul is under pressure to produce a résumé. Rival teachers have impressed some in the church, and Paul says he is "not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles."
Some readers hear a dry smile in that phrase. So he agrees to boast, warning everyone first that he's speaking like a fool. Then he writes a very strange résumé.

teach.b: Here's part of it, in the King James words: "Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep." He keeps going.
Dangers on rivers, from robbers, in the city, in the wilderness, at sea.
Then the ordinary misery of travel: "In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness." Read slowly, it stops sounding like a boast.
It sounds like someone emptying his pockets.

teach.h: THE CARE OF ALL THE CHURCHES.
teach.b: And after the stonings and shipwrecks comes the last item: "that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches." The final hardship isn't a wound. It's worry, lying awake over people he loves.
He counts that too. Then he says why he wrote the list at all: "If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities." Infirmities means weaknesses.
The next story he tells is almost funny. In Damascus the city was guarded to catch him, so he was let down through a window in the wall, in a basket.
That's where the chapter ends: a grown man lowered in a basket. Some readers put it this way: the point isn't that Paul was tough. It's that he was still there.
Beaten, cold, worried, smuggled out of a city, and still writing to the people he loved, still going.

how: Christians read Paul's hardship list in 2 Corinthians as a picture of faith that keeps going, and some turn to it in a long, hard season of their own.

o: the rules Paul set for anyone leading a church
a record of the churches and cities Paul founded
a boast made of hardships and weaknesses, not of wins

p: the care of all the churches
how he got out of Damascus

s: Paul lists his hardships to prove how strong he is
he says if he must boast, he'll boast of the things that concern his infirmities, his weaknesses.
Paul's list includes a night and a day in the deep
"thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep."
the last hardship on the list is a physical wound
it's the care of all the churches, which comes upon him daily.

games.q: you're Paul, in Damascus. the city is guarded to catch you. how do you get out?
o: fight your way through the gate.
get let down through a window in the wall, in a basket.
hide in the city until the guard gives up.
games.why: he's lowered through a window in the wall, in a basket, and escapes. it's how this part of his boast ends: not a victory, a basket.

practice: Quietly start your own strange résumé: not the wins, but the things you got through, a loss, an illness, a move you didn't want, a year that went wrong, and the worry that kept you up counts too, as it did for Paul.
Touch each one lightly, like counting on your fingers, without reliving it, and notice that you're here, on the other side of every one so far. If you pray, you can hand the list to God.

wordCard.voice: Paul's list. Beaten, shipwrecked, hungry, cold, worried, and still going. It closes a week that walked through patience, the race, courage, your own story, thanks, and joy in hard times.

orig.note: Greek: weakness. the King James calls it infirmities in 2 Corinthians 11:30.

carryVoice: Your line: still here. In Paul's list, weakness is nothing to hide. That's today, done.
